data.title: Nymex Overview: U.S. Crude Prices on Track to End Six-Day Streak of Increases — OPIS
data.description:
Crude-oil and refined product futures prices were falling, but most remained on track to post weekly gains.

The November West Texas Intermediate crude contract was down by 45cts to $97.52/bbl in light trade on Friday. The more-active December contract was down 88cts to $95.62/bbl. The front-month contract is currently nearly $6/bbl above last Friday's settlement.

December Brent crude was down by 18cts to $105.74/bbl while January prices were flat at $103.17/bbl. December prices are $1/bbl ahead for the week.

ULSD futures were on track for a second day of declines, with the November contract falling by 5.6cts to $4.7896/gal, still about 5cts ahead of last week's settlement. The more-active December contract was down by 4.37cts to $4.6108/gal.

Most activity in RBOB was also focused on the next-month contract, with November prices falling by 4.08cts to $3.1394/gal and December prices trading 2.7cts lower to $3.0528/gal. RBOB futures are on track to end the week about 15cts/gal lower than last Friday.

U.S. crude prices have seen a six-day streak of increases as supply concerns have supported the market. Friday's declines come even after the Energy Information Administration on Thursday reported a sharp 8.6 million-bbl drop in U.S. commercial crude inventories.

But those concerns are being mitigated by the announcement by the International Energy Agency that member countries have agreed to accelerate the release of 100 million bbls of crude oil and refined products that they had previously announced would be put into markets.

The release is expected to include about 20 million bbl of diesel.

The week's increase in diesel futures prices is being felt by consumers, with the average retail diesel price Friday of $6.3261/gal marking the fourth day of increases and an increase of about 5cts/gal from last Friday.

Gasoline prices around the country Friday averaged $4.3271/gal, about 6cts/gal lower than a week ago.

data.title: These S&P 500 stocks lead in capital efficiency - BofA
data.description:
Companies that generate high returns on fresh invested capital relative to their financing costs consistently beat the market over the long run, according to quantitative research from Bank of America.

BofA strategist Savita Subramanian highlighted that businesses producing more output per dollar of capital create structural shareholder value. Historical data show that companies ranking in the top sector-neutral decile for return on incremental invested capital relative to their weighted average cost of capital (ROIIC–WACC) have outpaced bottom-decile peers by around 1.6 percentage points annually since 1990.

Screening the non-financial constituents of the S&P 500 , BofA ranked the top decile of companies by their five-year ROIIC–WACC spread. Web services platform GoDaddy leads the ranking with a spread of 12.11, followed by industrials firm Illinois Tool Works at 6.92 and refiner Marathon Petroleum at 6.06.

data.title: Broker tips: Bridgepoint, Pulsar Helium
data.description:
Berenberg, which reiterated its 'buy' rating on the stock, said stronger‑than‑expected performance‑related earnings across FY26-28, driven initially by Energy Capital Partners Fund V and later by both ECP and private equity, had prompted the valuation change.

Bridgepoint has now upgraded guidance three times this year, with Berenberg stating the exceptional returns in ECP V were behind the FY26 PRE uplift, with one asset, ProEnergy, expected to deliver substantial carry on its own. PRE guidance for FY27-28 has also been raised, reflecting broader contributions from ECP funds and strong value creation in private equity.

Fundraising targets have been exceeded, highlighted Berenberg, with the increased €28bn goal for FY24-26 already being met and the total now expected to reach around €30bn.

Berenberg said the combination of higher management‑fee visibility and upgraded PRE across FY26-28 meant profits and cash generation should rise significantly.

Bridgepoint has rebased its FY26 dividend per share from 10p to 15p, equivalent to around 40% to 45% of EPS, and plans to distribute 40% to 60% of cash profits thereafter through ordinary dividends and top‑ups via specials or buybacks.

Berenberg noted that its fundraising assumptions were already close to the new guidance, so changes there were limited. However, the PRE upgrades drove a 40% increase to its FY26 EPS forecast and an 8% uplift for FY27, while dividend per share estimates rose 56% to 96% across FY26-28, in line with the updated distribution policy.

The German bank also raised the multiples used in its valuation framework, citing stronger fundraising, better‑than‑expected fund returns, higher embedded value, best‑in‑class underlying earnings margins and an enhanced capital‑distribution profile. FRE and PRE multiples moved from 12x/6x to 15x/7.5x, respectively.

Over at Canaccord Genuity, analysts initiated coverage of Pulsar Helium with a 'speculative buy' rating and a 150p target price on Friday, noting the group was advancing a major primary helium resource at its Topaz project in Minnesota.

The Canadian broker believes Topaz contains more than 1bn cubic feet of recoverable helium, well above the 380m cu ft P50 estimate in the 2024 CPR, after Pulsar successfully encountered helium in seven wells drilled to date.

Pulsar has lined up Chart Industries to supply equipment for a helium plant with around 5m cu meteres per year capacity and contracted up to six additional production wells, with total development costs estimated at $175m.

Canaccord said the tight global helium market - with around 25% of supply offline - supports strong pricing for years to come, and forecasts Pulsar generating over $130m in net profit from FY29 onwards.

First production was expected as early as Q1 2029, supported by recent legislative changes in Minnesota, with key catalysts ahead including a resource update, sales contracts and funding progress at Topaz.

Reporting by Iain Gilbert at Sharecast.com

data.title: Wall Street trades lower as tech struggles continue
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages were mixed on Friday as technology stocks came under further pressure amid an already challenging trading week.

The blue-chip Dow was last +0.5%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) was +0.1%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite was -0.4%.

From a sector-by-sector basis, nine of the 11 segments were in the green, led by materials. At the other end of the spectrum, info tech struggled the most.

A pullback in artificial intelligence-related stocks has weighed on the broader market this week, with memory chip stocks among the hardest-hit segments as investors reassessed the sector's recent performance.

On the economic calendar, industrial production growth accelerated more than expected in September. U.S. industrial production data rose 0.7% M/M in September, versus the 0.4% forecasted level.

The U.S. 2-year Treasury yield held even at 4.76%, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield ticked up 3 basis points to 5.11%, and the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield added 3 basis points to 5.44%.

“We think that investors should start thinking of a 5%+ 10-year Treasury yield as the new normal, not a brief aberration. For years, the Treasury enjoyed the luxury of having huge rate insensitive buyers, such as China, Japan, and the Fed, but those buyers are gone now and Treasuries have to offer competitive returns at a time when they are increasing supply due to the government’s profligate spending, which itself is giving creditors reason to require a higher rate of return,” Dennis Follmer of Montis Financial stated.

As for stocks that were on the move, shares of Nucor advanced +3.1%, while shares of CoreWeave fell -6%.

data.title: Copart Completes Acquisition Of ACV Auctions

WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - On Friday, Copart, Inc. (CPRT), an online vehicle auction company, announced the successful completion of its acquisition of ACV Auctions (ACVA).

Copart completed its tender offer to acquire ACV Auctions shares for $10.50 per share in cash. By the October 15, 2026 deadline, 116.8 million shares, representing 68.43% of ACV's outstanding shares, had been tendered and accepted for payment.

After the tender offer, Copart completed its acquisition of ACV Auctions through a merger. Remaining ACV shares were cancelled and converted into the right to receive $10.50 per share in cash, subject to applicable withholding taxes.

On the Nasdaq, shares of Copart were trading 0.13 percent higher at $27.78.

data.title: Big Tech Earnings Suddenly Matter for the Bond Market — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Martin Baccardax

"A funny thing happened to the bond market this week ..." It sounds like the opening line of a joke shared among traders on Wall Street, but it describes a notable shift in fixed-income sentiment that could signal trouble heading into the final stretch of the year.

Treasury bonds have rallied sharply over the past three days, with yields falling from an intraday high of 5.33% on Wednesday, following a September inflation report that showed quickening price pressures, to as low as 5.055% on Thursday amid a worrying selloff in tech stocks and the broader AI investment trade.

The shift is worth watching: Investors appear increasingly concerned about the economic fallout from a potentially lasting AI slump, even as rising global crude prices stoke inflation risks.

"By now it has become obvious to most that bonds are no longer correlated to crude prices, but in fact the Nasdaq," said BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky, noting the massive pullback in Treasury yields, with this week's rally the largest since February, and the corresponding slide in AI-related chip stocks.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index, the chip sector benchmark, has fallen for eight consecutive sessions, dragging it deeper into bear market territory and extending its longest losing streak since 2008.

And AI angst is permeating everything from an index tracking the Magnificent Seven tech giants, which has fallen 2.1% over the past two days, to the broader Nasdaq benchmark, which is down 2.4% for the week and has slipped into negative territory for the month.

Jonas Goltermann, chief markets economist at Capital Economics, says the bond market's fixation on all things tech this week is "a departure from recent norms" that could simply be the result of a surprise piece of economic data against a backdrop of investor uncertainty that has been building since the summer.

"That said, the combination of falling equity markets, tech underperformance, lower yields and a weaker dollar is precisely what we would expect to see if the AI equity boom were to unwind," he added. "Our view is that a more sustained drawdown is likely over the next year or so, and that it will be accompanied by a fall in Treasury yields."

Evidence of a sustained AI unwind remains limited, but recent market moves have been striking.

High yield bond spreads are widening, default protection costs for investment grade borrowers are increasing, and investors are rotating into non-tech sectors in search of defensive positioning.

Treasury yields, which move inversely to bond prices, are falling as investors seek safety amid concerns about the AI boom. Slower AI spending could also weaken growth and ease inflation, supporting Treasury prices. Corporate bonds face a different risk: worries about borrowers' ability to repay their debt are pushing credit spreads wider.

CoreWeave shares, meanwhile, have become a focal point for broader AI valuation concerns. They have plunged nearly 30% since their early October high, and traded near their lowest levels since late July in early Friday trading.

And warnings from Wall Street's most respected voices are starting to grow louder.

Legendary investor Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC earlier this week that stocks are likely to get a boost from the midterm elections in November, but added that "if I was looking at a year from now, 2027 is going to be a very challenging year."

That likely puts the tech sector's third quarter earnings season, which begins next week with updates from Meta Platforms and Tesla and follows through with Mag 7 names like Alphabet, Amazon, Apple and Microsoft before the end of the month, squarely in the frame.

But it might be those very earnings reports that ease investors' concerns about a valuation bubble brewing in the market's most important sector.

As 22V's Dennis DeBusschere notes, indexes are perhaps more reliant on tech stocks for the lion's share of overall earnings than they were at the peak of the dot-com boom in 2000.

"However, on valuation the comparison reverses," he said. "Large-cap earnings strength is still broad and the AI boom differs from 2000 because it is backed by earnings."

Furthermore, earnings forecasts for companies outside the Big Tech cohort are also improving, suggesting "analysts are now slightly more optimistic about the broader market than they have usually been relative to the mega-caps."

"The earnings support behind [the market's autumn rally] is broad, not limited to a handful of leaders, and that is the clearest difference from 2000," DeBusschere concluded.

Whether that will be enough to steady markets into the final stretch of the year remains to be seen, but the two biggest factors are likely to be Big Tech's earnings outlook set and the bond market's assessment of the credit risks tied to AI spending.

Ed Yardeni, founder and CEO of Yardeni Research, agrees this will a key investor focus, as "doubts about future returns are pushing up borrowing costs" and "investors may be lowering their economic growth expectations amid concerns that the AI boom could slow."

But a slowdown isn't what he expects.

"We are nowhere near ready to write off the AI investment boom," he said, arguing that strong hyperscaler cash flows and solid balance sheets "make their spending plans relatively insensitive to higher borrowing costs" while smaller rivals struggle.

"Demand for compute continues to outpace supply, while rising adoption should fuel further investment," he said. "We expect the hyperscalers to keep spending and the Roaring 2020s to keep roaring."

We'll know more about the latest market battle between bonds and big tech over the coming weeks. And it's going to be a good one.

Write to Martin Baccardax at martin.baccardax@barrons.com

data.title: Sanara MedTech/MiMedx deal spread widens on FTC second request

data.title: Many of 2026's hottest stocks have seen dramatic comedowns this week
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Many of the best-performing stocks of 2026 fell this week, while this year's biggest losers also changed course

These are two of the best-performing stocks of 2026, which reversed course to show significant declines this week.

This week's action in the stock market has reflected investors' concerns about higher long-term interest rates and a simmering of the AI infrastructure trade. But in an interesting twist, it has also featured a change in sentiment for this year's best and worst performers.

The bond market provided its own warning on what may be overexuberance for an industry group riding the artificial-intelligence build-out - neoclouds, which are pure-play providers of cloud services. These companies have seen revenue soar, but some investors are concerned that the inevitable growth in supply will lead to declining sales and fierce price competition for what will turn out to be a commoditized service.

CoreWeave's (CRWV) stock was down 15.1% for the week through Thursday, but a more painful sign came from the bond market. The company's bonds issued in April with a 9.75% coupon were trading for 81 cents on the dollar on Wednesday.

Despite some alarming headlines, the S&P 500 SPX was showing a modest 0.9% gain for the week through Thursday, excluding dividends, with all but three sectors rising. Among the S&P 500, 357 stocks were up for the week.

The worst-performing sector was information technology, which fell 3.9% for the week through Thursday, after rising 29.9% for 2026 through Friday, Oct. 9. And the iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX, which holds stocks of 30 chip makers and related companies, was down 8% for the week through Thursday.

2026 winners become this week's losers

We sorted the S&P 500 by stock-price changes for 2026 through Oct. 9, to illustrate investors' change in attitude this week. It turns out that among the 20 best performers through last week, all but three were down this week, and 11 of the stocks were down double digits.

data.title: Moderna falls ahead of cancer vaccine data next week
data.description:
After a more than sevenfold YTD jump, Moderna fell nearly 10% in afternoon trading on Friday, becoming the biggest decliner in the S&P 500 (SP500) as investors await detailed results from a late-stage trial of its personalized cancer shot, intismeran autogene, developed with Merck .

The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based biotech has already lost over 5% this week, a notable reversal of fortunes for a company that skyrocketed more than 170% in a single session in August following topline data from the Phase 3 trial named INTerpath-001.

At the time, the companies said the study, which tested intismeran with Merck’s anti-PD-1 therapy Keytruda in patients with melanoma whose tumors were completely resected, met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival.

The presentation scheduled for Oct. 24 at this year’s European Society for Medical Oncology Congress is expected to shed more light on INTerpath-001, which was the first trial of its kind to outperform Keytruda in an adjuvant setting for resected melanoma.

However, investors have become increasingly cautious of Moderna ahead of the readout, with Seeking Alpha analysts issuing multiple Hold and Sell ratings on the stock over the past few weeks. SA analyst Mike Zaccardi is the latest to issue a Hold recommendation, noting a valuation that “remains story-driven and speculative.”

data.title: Midday Markets Need to Know: Steel prices surge, diesel costs stay high, and more
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages were mixed on Friday as technology stocks came under further pressure amid an already challenging trading week.

Here are the four news items investors should watch:

U.S. steel prices hit four-year highs: The steel sector is set to report Q3 earnings in the coming days and weeks that analysts expect will show higher sales and profits, as U.S. steel prices have climbed to more than four-year highs. U.S. tariffs on imported steel are restricting foreign supply, which has helped boost U.S. hot-rolled coil prices by 52% over the past year to $1,255/short ton, the highest level since May 2022, Bloomberg reported Friday. The U.S. is a net importer of steel but deliveries of overseas supplies have declined sharply this year, as imports of finished steel fell 14% YTD to ~13M tons, resulting in a slide of imports' share of the domestic market to 16% from 19% for the same period last year, according to the American Iron and Steel Institute.

High global diesel prices and supply constraints: High global diesel prices and supply constraints are set to persist even as crude oil prices (, and (:COM) soften, according to Daan Struyven, Goldman Sachs co-head of global commodities research. In an interview with CNBC, Struyven noted that Goldman Sachs expects "somewhat lower crude prices" going forward but warned of "very high product prices for longer." U.S. average retail diesel prices recently hit an all-time high of $6.50 a gallon and remain just above $6, creating significant economic headwinds. Struyven described diesel as the "workhorse fuel of the global economy," explaining that unlike gasoline (XB1:COM) and jet fuel, "it has a very broad-based impact on many CPI categories."

Household debt delinquencies rise: The U.S. government isn't the only one with a debt problem. One in five Americans fell behind on a loan or mortgage payment in 2025, according to new data from the Federal Reserve that tracks the metrics every three years. That figure is up from one in eight Americans in 2022 and marks the highest level since 2007. Additionally, more than 8% of them reported being two months late or more, up from 5% in 2022. Interest rates for major types of household debt increased over the period of 2022 to 2025, with the average interest rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rising from 4.2% to 6.7% and the average new vehicle loan interest rate advancing from 4.9% to 7.7%.

Miami leads major metros in housing buyer imbalance: Miami was the strongest buyer’s market among the 10 leading U.S. metropolitan areas in September, with home sellers outnumbering buyers by 158.9%, according to Redfin data shared by Charlie Bilello. Miami had 18.9K home sellers compared with 7.3K buyers, the largest percentage gap in the ranking. Nashville, Tennessee, followed, with sellers outnumbering buyers by 152.3%, while Houston, Texas, ranked third at 134.6%. Nashville had 18.1K sellers and 7.2K buyers, while Houston recorded 47.5K sellers against 20,230 buyers. Although Houston had the largest number of sellers among the 10 markets, Miami had the widest relative gap between sellers and buyers.

data.title: LatAm FX mixed as investors eye polls on Brazil elections
data.description:
Key points:
  • IMF urges LatAm to cut debt, lift productivity while tailwinds last
  • Bolsonaro's lead over Lula narrows, polls this week show
  • World Bank sees up to $5 bln in possible loans to Venezuela, report says

By Sudeshna Ghoshal and Johann M Cherian

Most Latin American currencies were mixed on Friday, with the focus on Brazil as new polls showed both presidential candidates in a tight race, while investors also parsed index operator MSCI's warnings about Indonesia and Turkey's status as "emerging markets".

New polls this week showed the lead achieved by right-wing candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro during the first-round vote appeared to be dwindling into a technical tie with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the presidential race on October 25. The latest was a survey by CNT/MDA.

The real struggled to make strong gains and was last up 0.2% at 5 reals to the dollar, while the Bovespa index managed a 0.3% rise. However, both the assets were on course for weekly declines, with the currency and the equities benchmark set for their biggest weekly drop since mid-August.

Analysts also noted the significance of the government passing legislation that would reduce the country's workweek from six days to five.

"The passing of the labor reform, shortening the workweek, seems like a pro-Lula win even though plenty on the right agreed to also pass it," said Juan Perez, director of trading at Monex.

The elections are being closely watched by the United States and China, given Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America at a time when the region broadly has seen a right-wing sweep in governments.

"There is growing concern about a political crisis potentially forming as Brazil navigates two diplomatic policies: holding firm with China and keeping the US as a friend," Perez said.

Data showed economic activity in Brazil rose by a seasonally adjusted 0.3% in August from the previous month, matching the median forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.

SELLOFFS IN TURKEY, INDONESIA

Turkey and Indonesia were under scrutiny after index provider MSCI warned of downgrades from "emerging market" status, citing a lack of transparency over trading practices.

Turkish equities fell nearly 3%, while Indonesian stocks tanked 11.6% and logged their biggest daily drop since 1998.

More broadly, MSCI's LatAm currency index (.MILA00000CUS) shed 0.5%, with declines led by Mexico's peso , which slipped 0.4%, and Colombia's peso , which dipped 0.1%.

Mexico's equities benchmark gained 1.3%, with FEMSA up 5.4% after JPMorgan hiked its rating on the bottler and retailer's shares in New York.

Stalled progress on the US-Mexico-Canada free trade deal remains a key overhang for the country.

Against this backdrop, the International Monetary Fund urged Latin American governments to take advantage of still-favorable global conditions to cut public debt and raise productivity, while warning that a fiscal adjustment has stalled in many countries including Mexico, Brazil and Colombia.

For Venezuela, the World Bank said it sees up to $5 billion in possible loans to the country over the next two years, a report said.

VANCOUVER, BC, Oct. 16, 2026 /CNW/ -- Wondershare today announced the launch of Wondershare UniConverter 18, introducing new AI capabilities and workflow enhancements to its all-in-one media processing software. The update brings automated image enhancement, more flexible conversion workflows, improved processing performance, and expanded tools for downloading, enhancing, and editing media. Together, these enhancements help users manage diverse media tasks with greater efficiency and control.

AI-Powered Image and Video Enhancement

UniConverter 18 expands its image and video enhancement capabilities, helping users improve visual quality with less manual adjustment.

Auto Fix streamlines image enhancement by analyzing photos for issues such as blur, poor lighting, faded colors, and visible damage, then selecting a tailored enhancement approach for each image. This reduces the need for users to compare enhancement models manually. UniConverter 18 also improves the efficiency of generative video upscaling and enhances portrait processing consistency in challenging situations, including out-of-focus or partially obscured faces.

More Efficient Workflows and Greater Control Over Output

The update improves conversion automation, processing performance, and output control to support more flexible and efficient media workflows.

Watch Folder automatically converts new files added to designated folders according to predefined rules, supporting recurring workflows such as processing incoming footage and maintaining media libraries.

UniConverter 18 also introduces AI Media Agent, which allows users to initiate batch media conversion tasks using natural-language instructions.

Goal-based compression settings let users set a target file size, compression ratio, or quality level to meet specific delivery requirements. Audio Passthrough preserves compatible original audio streams without re-encoding in supported workflows. Additional updates include CPU usage control and improved preservation of supported audio and subtitle tracks.

Under the hood, UniConverter 18 upgrades GPU processing pipelines for NVIDIA-powered Windows systems and optimizes HDR processing on Windows and macOS. In selected Windows GPU conversion tests without additional editing operations, these upgrades reduced processing time by up to approximately 90% compared with the previous version. The improvements help users process supported media more efficiently, with actual results varying by hardware, source files, and conversion settings.

Expanded Tools for Downloading, Editing, and Managing Media

UniConverter 18 broadens its media toolkit with enhanced downloading options, more precise video cleanup, and additional image-enhancement capabilities.

The update expands downloading options to include eligible YouTube account content, such as Watch Later and Liked videos, subject to login and access permissions. Users can download supported video chapters as individual files or save the full video . The update also adds M3U8 stream downloading and supports selecting multiple available language tracks when downloading YouTube subtitles.

For video cleanup, Video Blur uses face detection and object tracking to obscure selected areas throughout footage. Precise Subtitle Removal identifies embedded subtitles and their appearance intervals to help target unwanted text. Enhancements to Video Eraser improve the removal of unwanted objects and moving subjects, along with background reconstruction.

"As digital content continues to grow in volume and diversity, users need more intelligent and efficient ways to manage increasingly complex media workflows," said Desmond Ye, Product Director of Wondershare UniConverter. "With UniConverter 18, we are advancing our vision of AI-powered media processing by bringing greater intelligence and automation to everyday tasks. We aim to make powerful media technologies more accessible, helping users streamline their workflows, achieve their desired results, and unlock greater value from their content."

With AI-assisted processing, automated conversion, and expanded media tools, Wondershare UniConverter 18 helps users handle diverse media tasks through a more connected and flexible workflow.

data.title: Michael Dell, a Dot-Com Era Survivor, Has Tips to Beat an AI Bust — WSJ
data.description:
By Christopher Mims

Spooked investors are fleeing some of the big-tech companies that reached new highs on the back of the artificial-intelligence boom.

But Michael Dell says his company is well-placed to weather a storm. The direct-to-consumer PC company he founded in a dorm room in 1984 with $1,000 has pivoted to delivering the powerful supercomputers that tech giants can't get enough of. And its strategy for selling them makes it relatively unique among the businesses benefiting most from the world's unprecedented AI infrastructure build-out.

Dell relies on just-in-time manufacturing of its AI servers and PCs, which has allowed it, in essence, to get its customers to finance its operations and inventory. Meanwhile, hyperscalers like Amazon.com and Google and the builders of their AI data centers — the so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius and Crusoe — are piling on debt to fund the build-out of their AI hubs.

Dell Technologies' valuation is almost four times what it was a year ago, boosted by a projected 70% increase in revenue for its current fiscal year.

When I asked Dell on Tuesday about how he was preparing his company for a possible downturn in the AI cycle, he said, "There are some new challenges that this presents, but if you look at our cash conversion cycle, it's still negative."

Translation: Dell manufactures powerful AI servers only when customers order them. And by taking payment from customers upfront, and extending the period over which it pays its vendors, Dell is able to sit on those payments for days or even weeks, giving it a cash cushion and insulating it from the risk of holding too much inventory.

Dell has plenty of competitors selling big, powerful computers, including Super Micro, HPE and Lenovo. But it's the leader in providing the brains of modern data centers to enterprise customers who want to build their own AI.

Dell said it took the company eight quarters to amass 3,200 customers building AI data centers with its servers, including Elon Musk's SpaceX. In the last three quarters, it added 3,300 more.

Two days after we talked, the market sent the company's stock down by more than 10%. The rest of its cohort — chip manufacturers, neoclouds and tech giants alike — also lost ground.

If that selloff continues and customers pull back, Dell's just-in-time inventory strategy makes the company something of a bellwether of the health of the rest of the AI-infrastructure boom. Lower revenue could show up almost immediately.

For now, Dell says his company is doing fine. It has $95 billion in back-orders for the powerful racks of AI servers — think of them as AI supercomputers, each weighing 3,000 pounds and drawing as much power as 100 or more typical U.S. households. The real bottleneck remains getting enough memory chips to deliver all those servers, says Dell. Next year, based on what Dell currently sees, "It's gonna get worse."

It's telling that one of the few other CEOs who was also an executive during the dot-com bust has adopted a similar strategy to Dell: Corning's Wendell Weeks. The company, which saw its revenue and stock price boom during the dot-com era, and then collapse along with the fiber build-out, has signed deals with Nvidia, Amazon and Meta Platforms in which those companies help finance the expanded manufacturing capacity for its fiber optics.

Corning doesn't have a negative cash-conversion cycle. When you make things from raw materials like sand, that's almost impossible. But its approach does mean that if the AI boom goes bust, its partners can't just walk away from the factories Corning had to build or expand.

Looking at models like the one Dell enjoys provides a useful way to game out a potential collapse. What might happen to each company in the AI supply chain if things don't go to plan? What if the $3.5 trillion in consumer and business spending on AI that will be required by 2032 to justify current investment doesn't materialize?

The longest-serving CEO of any Fortune 500 company to still be at it, and one of the wealthiest people on earth, Dell's winning streak in the AI boom thus far has made him a ubiquitous figure.

He's received a signed AI server from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a shout-out from Musk on X for appearing in a hard hat at a SpaceX data-center construction site. He recently went to the White House to receive a medal from President Trump, alongside Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and others.

His company's ability to rapidly scale production up or down, without being left holding suddenly worthless inventory, is just one of the reasons Dell told me he feels optimistic about the future despite the recent market selloff and memory woes.

The other, he told me during his visit to The Wall Street Journal, was more philosophical. He and his wife recently donated $6.25 billion to fund Trump accounts for 25 million children, and he said he plans to give away nearly all of his wealth within his lifetime.

"I mean, you can't take it with you."

Write to Christopher Mims at christopher.mims@wsj.com

data.title: NEC Develops VLM Technologies That Accurately Identify Small-Scale Damage in Disaster Site Images and Adapt to New Types of Damage
data.description:
TOKYO, Oct 16, 2026 - (JCN Newswire) - NEC Corporation (NEC; TSE: 6701) has developed two new technologies for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLM-based Local Region Understanding (*1) and Continual Learning for VLMs (*2), which are expected to be utilized in rescue operations and recovery efforts by local governments and other organizations. VLM-based Local Region Understanding accurately identifies small-scale damage visible within images collected from disaster sites. Continual Learning for VLMs enables new types of damage information to be added as search criteria while maintaining the VLM's original recognition capabilities. These technologies are the result of joint research with the Okatani Laboratory at Tohoku University in Japan.

VLMs are expected to support rescue and recovery efforts by enabling users to search for large volumes of images using natural language and efficiently narrow down the images that match specific situations. NEC's technologies not only reduce the likelihood of overlooking small-scale damage but also allow search criteria to be added later. In NEC's verification, they reduced the time required to identify specific disaster conditions to less than an hour, which previously took approximately 7 hours by visual inspection (*3). Through these technologies, NEC aims to contribute to speeding up disaster response by local governments and other organizations, with practical implementation targeted for fiscal year 2027.

Background

In recent years, as natural disasters have become more severe and frequent, the importance of minimizing damage and making rapid decisions has increased. There are often tens of thousands of on-site images immediately after a disaster occurs, but it takes an enormous amount of effort and time for staff to visually inspect them. Against this backdrop, there are high expectations for VLMs that can identify relevant images based on textual queries to enable even small teams to quickly assess disaster situations.

However, many types of damage critical to rescue and recovery decisions appear only as small details within images, occupying 10% or less of an image's area, and conventional VLMs sometimes overlook them (*4). Furthermore, while VLMs excel at recognizing common objects and situations, they can struggle to identify previously unseen phenomena, such as region-specific events like landslides and flooding, or newly identified damage. Moreover, additional training can reduce the accuracy of previously recognized events (forgetting).

To address these challenges, NEC developed VLM-based Local Region Understanding, which comprehends even the finest details of images, and Continual Learning for VLMs, which adds new information while retaining existing knowledge. These research findings were accepted as papers and presented at the international computer vision conferences "ECCV 2024" and "ECCV 2026."

Value Proposition

These technologies reduce the likelihood of overlooking small-scale damage visible in field images and cut the time required to assess specific damage conditions to less than an hour, which previously took personnel approximately 7 hours to complete visually. During the initial response phase immediately following a disaster, they accelerate assessment through text-based searches (e.g., "roads blocked by landslide debris"). When making recovery decisions, they help prioritize on-site inspections by sorting out images of damage to roads and buildings. Furthermore, search criteria can be continuously added to enable flexible responses to unforeseen disaster risks-such as flooding following an earthquake-and to local conditions.

Features of This Technology

1. High-precision detection of even the finest details in images, such as small areas and narrow regions

NEC's proprietary VLM-based Local Region Understanding incorporates region information of objects within an image into the VLM's feature extraction process, enabling it to extract information by focusing not only on the entire image but also on small areas and narrow regions. As a result, NEC has confirmed that even small areas accounting for 10% or less of an image can be identified with the same level of accuracy that conventional VLMs achieve for areas accounting for about 30-40% of an image. This enables the technology to accurately identify even small-scale damage, such as partial structural damage to buildings or cracks in roads, and to generate detailed descriptions.

2. New information can be added while maintaining the recognition capabilities of the existing VLM

NEC's proprietary Continual Learning for VLMs uses not only additional training data, but also a diverse range of descriptions generated by the VLM itself before additional training. By learning from both sources together, the system can recognize new events while minimizing any decline in the accuracy for previously recognized events. Since there is no need to prepare a large volume of historical training data, search criteria can be added repeatedly at a later stage. This allows images to be narrowed down using both newly learned disaster-related events and existing features such as mountains and rivers as clues; in NEC's verification experiments, this reduced the number of images requiring final human verification from 5,035 to an average of 544 (about one-ninth), cutting the review time to less than an hour (*3).

Through these technologies, NEC will help local governments and other organizations quickly assess disaster situations. Going forward, in addition to ground-level site images, NEC will combine these technologies with the analysis of wide-area observation data, such as optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite imagery, to support a multifaceted understanding of disaster conditions, and will advance research and development aimed at preventing disasters before they occur.

(*1) A technology that incorporates region information of objects in an image into the VLM's feature extraction process, enabling image understanding focused on small objects and limited regions. Presented at the European Conference on Computer Vision 2024 (ECCV 2024). [N. Sogi, T. Shibata, and M. Terao, "Object-aware query perturbation for cross-modal image-text retrieval," Proc. ECCV, pp. 447-464, 2024.]

(*2) A technology that adds new knowledge while suppressing the forgetting of existing knowledge by taking into account, during training, descriptions generated by the VLM before additional training. Presented at the European Conference on Computer Vision 2026 (ECCV 2026). Its effectiveness in suppressing forgetting was confirmed in evaluations on public datasets. [N. Sogi, R. Ohkubo, T. Shibata, M. Terao, Y. Hosoya, and T. Okatani, "CaPCL: Caption-preserved continual learning for text-to-image retrieval," Proc. ECCV, 2026.]

(*3) Based on NEC verification using 5,035 vehicle-mounted camera images extracted from archival footage of the Great East Japan Earthquake, covering 12 types of disaster-related events. Visually inspecting all images at 5 seconds per image takes approximately 7 hours. Applying these technologies narrows the images for each target event to an average of 544, reducing the time to approximately 45 minutes (less than an hour).

(*4) Based on NEC verification. In the image dataset used, the target damage occupied 10% or less of the image area in approximately 60% of cases.

About NEC

The NEC Group leverages technology to create social value and promote a more sustainable world where everyone has the chance to reach their full potential. NEC Corporation was established in 1899. Today, the NEC Group's approximately 110,000 employees utilize world-leading AI, security, and communications technologies to solve the most pressing needs of customers and society.

For more information, please visit https://www.nec.com, and follow us on LinkedIn and YouTube.

data.title: Investors Unmoved by High-Flying Tesla Roadster Debut — WSJ
data.description:
By Patrick George

Elon Musk may have dazzled the internet with Thursday's gravity-defying debut of the thruster-equipped Tesla Roadster, but Wall Street was less enthusiastic on Friday.

The Musk-run automaker showed off an angular, ultra-fast sports car it says will be capable of flight via "cold-air thrusters" supposedly derived from SpaceX technology.

Yet Tesla shares are trading down more than 1%, indicating investors aren't especially moved by the long-term growth of flying vehicles from the company.

Tesla in recent years has affirmed that its future lies not in making cars, but in developing autonomous vehicles, AI and humanoid robotics. Much of the company's sky-high valuation-eclipsing dozens of other automakers put together-comes from its autonomy efforts.

However, the vast majority of Tesla's revenue comes from selling cars. An ultra-high-end car like the Roadster is expected to be expensive. (Its final price tag wasn't released, but it won't be cheap.)

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," wrote Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives in a note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack" ahead of next week's third-quarter earnings.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Arizona approves state's first non-ABA accredited law school
data.description:
By Karen Sloan

The Arizona Supreme Court has approved the state's first law school not accredited by the American Bar Association, a move the court said would help address Arizona's lawyer shortage.

The court's approval on Thursday of Grand Canyon University Law School, which is slated to open as early as fall 2027, means its graduates will be eligible to take Arizona's bar exam and apply to become licensed to practice in the state.

Grand Canyon law graduates would largely be limited to Arizona under current attorney licensing rules in other states that require graduation from an ABA-accredited law school, though some states have begun to relax that provision.

Officials at the private, Christian university said the school plans to pursue ABA accreditation but that Arizona's recognition will give it more flexibility amid potential changes to the bar association's status as the federally recognized accreditor of law schools.

The US Department of Education under President Donald Trump is poised to revoke the ABA's accreditor status, and five Republican-controlled states including Texas and Florida have moved to end their near-exclusive reliance on the ABA in attorney admissions.

James Williams, the founding dean of Grand Canyon's law school, in a statement said the school is grateful for the Arizona Supreme Court's "willingness to consider an innovative approach to legal education and for the opportunity to demonstrate that a new pathway to licensure can maintain the highest standards of academic excellence."

The court said it is not accepting approval requests from other non-ABA-accredited law schools while it assesses how its new approach is working.

Grand Canyon, located in Phoenix, unveiled plans for its new law school in August, saying it will "integrate the Christian worldview throughout its curriculum while emphasizing Constitutional law, free-market principles and the rule of law."

Grand Canyon will be the state's third law school alongside Arizona State University Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law and the University of Arizona James E. Rogers College of Law, both of which are accredited by the ABA.

A 2020 study by the ABA found that Arizona was tied with South Carolina and Arkansas for the lowest ratio of active attorneys per capita, with just 2.1 attorneys for every 1,000 Arizonans. The national average was roughly four lawyers per 1,000 residents.

The Arizona Supreme Court in 2024 established the Arizona Lawyers Apprentice Program, a first-of-its-kind effort that gives law school graduates who fall just short of passing the state's bar exam the option to become licensed attorneys after spending two years working under the supervision of a lawyer in a rural area or a government or nonprofit law setting.
